unit_result_entry.title: Rate of radius decay controls real analyticity versus entire density extension
unit_result_entry.why_material: Allocating successive small-radius factors in the characteristic-function products produces exponential Fourier decay; geometric-rate radius decay yields local real analyticity, while supergeometric decay permits arbitrarily strong exponential decay and entire extension in the two real coordinates.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: A nondegenerate double representation transfers positivity to the derivative-weighted density
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Two small circular summands are chosen so the same value has two regular phase preimages with distinct derivative weights; inverse-coordinate maps and a Jacobian lower bound prevent cancellation, reducing positivity of the weighted density G to the already-established positivity of an unweighted tail density.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: Independence factorizes characteristic functions; allocating enough small factors yields polynomial decay and arbitrary smoothness, while quantitative radius decay upgrades this to exponential decay and analytic or entire density extension.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The weighted law requires additional marked-factor summability, and exact decay rates depend on the radius sequence.
related_synthesis_entries.title: Fourier factor allocation yields a hierarchy from smoothness to entire density

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The rate at which component radii shrink is converted into a regularity scale. Assigning successively smaller factors to a large frequency forces the characteristic-function products to decay exponentially; a geometric rate gives a fixed exponential type and real analyticity, while supergeometric decay gives every exponential rate and hence entire extension.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The proof starts from the product representations for A(y;μ) and A(y;ν). With b defined by the limsup geometric rate of r_n, any a>b eventually bounds r_n by a^n. The local bound for K_0 supplies roughly one inverse-frequency contribution per allocated small factor; multiplying these bounds and using Stirling produces O(e^{-c|y|}) decay for the products, with a corresponding polynomial prefactor absorbed in the weighted sums. If b=0, c can be taken arbitrarily large. Fourier inversion then yields real analyticity in the first case and an entire function of the two real-coordinate variables in the second.
directed.conceptual_reading: This is a quantitative refinement of the earlier smoothness argument: factor abundance controls polynomial decay, but factor scale controls exponential decay. The asymptotic geometry of the radius sequence therefore becomes the analytic continuation budget of the density.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge runs from radius decay to factorwise Fourier decay, from the product to global exponential frequency decay, and then through Fourier inversion to spatial analyticity or entire extension.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The conclusion depends on the explicit product and marked-product formulas and their summability; a qualitative statement r_n→0 alone only supports smoothness, not analyticity. The weighted transform must absorb its marked-factor polynomial growth.
directed.uncertainty: The OCR corrupts the exact hypothesis as printed and several constants in the limsup estimate. The geometric-versus-supergeometric dichotomy and its Fourier-decay proof are explicit and agree with the bounded dossier.

supported: The proof allocates successive K_0 factors, applies their inverse-frequency bound, uses a factorial/Stirling estimate to obtain exponential decay of the unweighted and marked products, and transfers that decay by Fourier inversion to real analyticity or entire extension.
The weighted marked sums carry an additional polynomial factor that is explicitly absorbed by the exponential bound.
inference: Viewing the radius sequence as an analytic-continuation budget is a useful abstraction once the direction and scale of the rate hypothesis are stated correctly.
unsupported_or_imported: The candidate reconstructs b as a limsup geometric root, asserts an eventual bound r_n by a^n, and labels the cases geometric versus supergeometric radius decay. The frozen proof instead compares the reciprocal radius to the linear n scale: its displayed chain uses b=limsup r_n^{-1}/n and r_n^{-1}<an, matching the theorem's O(n) versus o(n) conditions. The candidate's version reverses the operative size relation and is not supported by the span.
paraphrase_or_style_risk: The polished geometric/supergeometric dichotomy appears to follow the dossier title rather than the proof's actual inequalities.
context_or_ocr_risk: The theorem hypothesis is OCR-damaged, so an exact symbolic reuse should be scan-verified; nevertheless, the subsequent b, an, t, and Stirling calculation rules out the candidate's a^n reconstruction.
missed_mechanism: The key distinction is not merely 'faster shrinkage gives stronger analyticity'; the proof needs enough factors with radii large enough at a given frequency, encoded by linear or sublinear growth of r_n^{-1}.
revision_instructions: Replace every geometric/supergeometric and a^n claim with the source-supported reciprocal-radius conditions: r_n^{-1}=O(n) for real analyticity and r_n^{-1}=o(n) for entire extension; describe b and the eventual inequality on the linear n scale. Preserve scan uncertainty for exact typography while retaining the valid factor-allocation, Stirling, exponential-decay, and Fourier-inversion mechanism.

unit_result_entry.title: Zeros of zeta-minus-value and log-zeta-minus-value have unbounded normalized totals over the half-plane
unit_result_entry.why_material: Theorem 15 condenses the boundary growth of Jensen slopes into the conclusion that the normalized number of relevant zeros in Re(s)>1/2 tends to infinity for log zeta minus arbitrary x and zeta minus nonzero x.

unit_dependency_entry.context_note: This is a source-level consequence of Theorems 13 and 14, not a Riemann-hypothesis claim.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Zeta-value density is Jensen curvature and determines motions and zero frequencies
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Theorem 14 gives the parallel statements for zeta minus x: asymptotic distribution, logarithmic-potential Jensen formula, curvature from the weighted zeta-value density, mean motions, and density-integral zero frequencies; its proof uses the exponential pushforward and relates zeta Jensen functions to all logarithmic preimages.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: As the log-Euler variance diverges at Re(s)=1/2, pointwise density flattens while the logarithmic-potential/Jensen quantities grow, producing increasing zero frequencies across the full half-plane.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The source establishes asymptotic distribution and zero-frequency consequences in Re(s)>1/2, not any assertion about the location of zeta zeros on the critical line.
related_synthesis_entries.title: Boundary variance collapse drives Jensen growth near the critical-line edge

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The final corollary converts boundary growth of the preceding Jensen slopes into a global abundance statement: when the whole half-plane to the right of one-half is allowed, the zero count grows faster than any fixed linear normalization. It is a cumulative consequence of strip-frequency formulas, not a new localization theorem.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Theorem 15 states that N(T)/T→∞ when N(T) counts either zeros of log ζ(s)-x in the relevant branch portion of Re(s)>1/2 for arbitrary x, or zeros of ζ(s)-x in Re(s)>1/2 for nonzero x. It is presented as a corollary of Theorems 13 and 14.
directed.conceptual_reading: Finite-strip densities of zeros are accumulated while the left boundary approaches the variance-divergent edge. The unbounded normalized total records growth of the integrated Jensen curvature across the entire open half-plane.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge is the preceding identity between strip zero frequency and the integral of the derivative-weighted value density. Boundary divergence lets those finite-strip frequencies become unbounded as strips exhaust Re(s)>1/2.
directed.boundary_or_failure: This is not a Riemann-hypothesis statement, does not place zeros on Re(s)=1/2, and does not say that every fixed strip has infinite normalized frequency. The zeta-minus-value statement excludes x=0, while the log-zeta statement retains its branch-domain restriction.
directed.uncertainty: The span is short and delegates its proof to Theorems 13 and 14. The half-plane symbol is OCR-degraded, but the dossier and surrounding theorem statements identify it as Re(s)>1/2.

supported: The short span explicitly states, as a corollary of Theorems 13 and 14, that N(T)/T tends to infinity for zeros of log zeta minus arbitrary x in the specified branch portion of the half-plane, and for zeros of zeta minus nonzero x in that half-plane.
The candidate correctly preserves the nonzero-target restriction for zeta and denies any Riemann-hypothesis or critical-line localization conclusion.
inference: It is reasonable to describe this as a cumulative rather than a new localization theorem because the source labels it a corollary.
unsupported_or_imported: The claims that finite-strip densities are accumulated, that integrated Jensen curvature is the operative quantity, and that boundary divergence makes strip frequencies unbounded are not present in this frozen eight-line span or its bounded nearby context. They are mechanisms imported from the preceding theorems, whose details this unit merely cites.
paraphrase_or_style_risk: Because the source unit contains only the corollary statement, adding a detailed curvature mechanism creates false depth unless the supporting theorem spans are explicitly reopened.
context_or_ocr_risk: The half-plane bound is OCR-degraded, although the assignment context identifies it; the exact theorem statement otherwise remains readable.
revision_instructions: Restrict the interpretation to the explicit N(T)/T conclusion, its two target cases, its status as a corollary, and its non-localization boundary. Remove the finite-strip, curvature-integral, and boundary-slope mechanism, or reopen and cite the exact supporting spans before retaining it.
